biography.currentRole: Governor of Texas (January 2015 - present); seeking fourth term in 2026
biography.education: B.B.A. Finance, University of Texas at Austin; J.D., Vanderbilt University Law School
biography.background: Conservative Republican. Became paraplegic after a tree fell on him during a jog in 1984. Known for aggressive use of state lawsuit power as AG (sued Obama administration 31 times). Three-term incumbent governor with an extensive executive record. Has signed approximately 24+ pro-gun bills, the nation's largest school voucher program ($1B ESA), total abortion ban, and constitutional ban on state income tax. Presides over $105.7M+ 2026 campaign war chest — a new Texas gubernatorial fundraising record. If he completes a fourth term, he would become Texas's longest-serving governor ever.

campaignWebsite.notes: Website confirmed live. Campaign issues page verified via web search. Direct fetch unavailable; positions extracted from campaign website coverage and campaign launch reporting.

statedPositions.quote: No income tax in Texas. The Texas House just passed a resolution to constitutionally ban an income tax in Texas.
statedPositions.notes: Constitutional amendment banning state income tax. 2026 centerpiece: eliminate school district property taxes for homeowners via constitutional amendment.

statedPositions.quote: It's time to drive a stake through the heart of local property tax hikes for good.
statedPositions.notes: Five-point property tax reform plan: cap local government spending growth at population+inflation or 3.5%; require 2/3 voter approval for all local tax hikes; cap appraisal growth at 3%; appraise all properties once every 5 years; ultimately eliminate school district property taxes for homeowners. School funding shifted to state-level sales/surplus revenues.

statedPositions.quote: Governor Abbott has taken unprecedented steps to secure our southern border, including busing migrants to sanctuary cities like Washington D.C., building the Texas border wall, declaring Mexican drug cartels as terrorist organizations, and seizing enough lethal doses of fentanyl through Operation Lone Star.
statedPositions.notes: Campaign website issues page. Explicit enforcement-first immigration approach. Texas has spent $11B+ on border operations.

statedPositions.quote: School choice equals competition, and competition will make all schools better — schools, charter schools and home schools.
statedPositions.notes: Reaffirmed at 2026 campaign launch. Already signed $1B ESA (voucher) law in May 2025.

statedPositions.quote: As long as I am governor of the great state of Texas, Texas will always protect the unborn.
statedPositions.notes: Reaffirmed at 2026 Texas Rally for Life. Texas has total abortion ban with no exceptions for rape/incest. Abbott signed SB8, trigger law, and 2025 mail-order pill ban.

statedPositions.quote: Abbott has signed nearly two dozen pro-gun bills into law, including House Bill 1927 which made Texas the 21st constitutional carry state in the nation.
statedPositions.notes: NRA endorsement language. A+ NRA grade confirmed through 2026 cycle.

statedPositions.quote: Governor Abbott highlights banning DEI, reforming bail system, prohibiting cities from defunding police.

keyActions.action: Signed HB 1927 — Constitutional/Permitless Carry
keyActions.notes: Made Texas the 21st constitutional carry state. Removed license and training requirements for handgun carry. NRA CEO Wayne LaPierre attended signing ceremony at the Alamo.

keyActions.action: Signed 7-bill gun rights package
keyActions.notes: Package included: SB 19 (bans government contracting with firms boycotting gun industry), SB 20 (hotel firearm storage rights), SB 550 (holster requirement removal), HB 957, HB 1500, HB 2622. Comprehensive expansion of gun rights with no new safety measures.

keyActions.action: Signed SB 8 — Texas Heartbeat Act (6-week abortion ban)
keyActions.notes: Private enforcement mechanism allowed any person to sue providers. No exceptions for rape or incest. Abbott defended the absence of exceptions by stating Texas would 'eliminate all rapists from the streets' — claim later fact-checked as misleading.

keyActions.action: Signed HB 1280 — Abortion Trigger Ban
keyActions.notes: Activated August 25, 2022 after Dobbs decision. Near-total ban; criminal penalties for providers. No rape/incest exceptions.

keyActions.action: Signed Life of the Mother Act (SB 31 and SB 33)
keyActions.notes: Clarified medical exceptions to give doctors more legal clarity for emergency procedures (e.g., premature rupture of membranes, ectopic pregnancies). Does NOT add rape/incest exceptions. Bipartisan support, championed by a Houston Democratic lawmaker.

keyActions.action: Signed HB 7 — Mail-order abortion pill ban
keyActions.notes: Effective December 4, 2025. Bans mailing of abortion pills into Texas. Allows citizens to sue anyone who distributes them.

keyActions.action: Launched Operation Lone Star — $11B+ state border enforcement program
keyActions.notes: Joint DPS/National Guard operation. Claimed 527,600+ apprehensions, 49,000+ criminal arrests, 573M+ lethal doses of fentanyl seized. Bused 119,200 migrants to Democratic cities (NYC, Chicago, DC, Denver). Built border wall segments. ACLU found ~70% of arrests were misdemeanor charges. Courts invalidated many early arrests as discriminatory. Abbott requested $11.1B federal reimbursement.

keyActions.action: Signed ESA (school voucher) bill — $1 billion Education Savings Accounts
keyActions.notes: Nation's largest school voucher program. $10K/student, $30K for special needs students, $2K for homeschoolers. Abbott ousted 11 Republican legislators who voted against school vouchers in 2024 primaries before finally passing. Starts issuing funds 2026-27 school year.

keyActions.action: Signed SB 17 — DEI Ban at public universities
keyActions.notes: Second state in the country to ban DEI offices at public universities. Effective January 1, 2024.

keyActions.action: Signed SB 12 and SB 13 — Parental Bill of Rights (2025)
keyActions.notes: Banned instruction on LGBTQ+ 'harmful sexual orientation and gender identity concepts' in public schools. Framed as parental rights.

keyActions.action: Signed HB 900 — School library book restriction
keyActions.notes: Bans sexually explicit materials from school libraries. Vendors must rate books for sexual content.

keyActions.action: Signed HB 1900 and SB 23 — Anti-defunding-police legislation
keyActions.notes: HB 1900 froze property tax revenues for cities over 250K population that defund police; cities also lose annexation powers for 10 years. SB 23 requires voter approval to reduce law enforcement budgets in counties 1M+. Most punitive anti-defund law in the country.

keyActions.action: Pledged and executed pardon of Daniel Perry (convicted of murdering BLM protester)
keyActions.notes: Abbott pledged pardon one day after Perry was convicted of murder for shooting Garrett Foster at a 2020 BLM protest. Executed pardon May 2024 after board recommendation. Perry had made racist text messages before the shooting. Travis County DA attempted to overturn the pardon. Heavily criticized as politically injecting into the criminal justice system.

keyActions.action: Executive Order GA-34 — Lifted statewide mask mandate, opened Texas 100%
keyActions.notes: 'Going forward, in Texas, there will not be any government-imposed shutdowns or mask mandates.' One of the earliest states to fully open. Abbott's rationale: individual liberty.

keyActions.action: Executive Orders GA-39 and GA-40 — Banned COVID-19 vaccine mandates statewide
keyActions.notes: Banned any entity in Texas — including private employers — from requiring COVID-19 vaccination. Prohibited vaccine passport requirements. Called Biden administration vaccine policy 'federal government overreach.' Later codified by Texas legislature.

keyActions.action: Opposed Medicaid expansion — held firm throughout three terms
keyActions.notes: Called Medicaid expansion 'a tax increase waiting to happen' and Medicaid 'broken and bloated.' Texas has the nation's highest uninsured rate (~16%). Has led multiple lawsuits to strike down the ACA — first as AG (2010) and again as governor.

keyActions.action: Signed Texas Pharmaceutical Initiative (SB 2402) and drug price transparency law
keyActions.direction: moderate — transparency/market mechanism, not price controls
keyActions.notes: Creates statewide PBM focused on price transparency and savings. Develops manufacturing partnerships for generic/specialty drugs. Requires manufacturers, PBMs, and health plans to report aggregate price data. Framed as market-based tool, not government price controls. More moderate than typical Republican posture on healthcare costs.

keyActions.action: Vowed to exclude renewables from Chapter 313 replacement economic incentive program
keyActions.notes: Stated explicitly: 'I support [the program] not providing economic incentives for renewables.' Focus on 'dispatchable power' (natural gas/coal). Introduced 5 bills penalizing wind/solar and subsidizing natural gas.

keyActions.action: Signed SB 13 — Anti-ESG fossil fuel investment mandate
keyActions.notes: Required state pension funds to divest from firms 'boycotting' fossil fuels. Struck down as unconstitutional by a federal judge in February 2026 (First Amendment grounds). Abbott has not publicly responded to the ruling.

keyActions.action: Executive order to protect Texas energy industry from federal ESG/climate overreach
keyActions.notes: Directed all state agencies to use all lawful powers to challenge any federal climate action threatening Texas energy sector. Consistent with AG-era EPA lawsuit record.

keyActions.action: Vetoed energy efficiency bill
keyActions.notes: Vetoed legislation that would have required energy efficiency standards.

keyActions.action: Post-ERCOT Winter Storm Uri response: signed SB 2 and SB 3 grid reform
keyActions.notes: Required weatherization of all generation types but Abbott's policy response was fossil-fuel-focused: $18B for 10 new gas plants (zero-interest loans at taxpayer expense). Abbott initially blamed wind/solar for the crisis — this was disputed by experts (gas infrastructure failed more). FERC final report confirmed unwinterized fossil fuel plants caused most blackouts.

keyActions.action: Signed housing supply reform bills — SB 840, SB 15, HB 24
keyActions.direction: poleA lean (loosen zoning / more supply) via market deregulation
keyActions.notes: SB 840: allows multifamily housing on any commercially-zoned land without rezoning; prohibits density/parking restrictions; minimum 36 units/acre. SB 15: prohibits unreasonably large lot requirements on 5-acre+ tracts. HB 24: reforms valid petition process so small groups cannot block pro-housing zoning changes. Abbott statement: 'This session, Texas did more than any state in America to make housing more affordable.' Bipartisan support. Pew Charitable Trusts applauded. Market-supply-side approach, not government subsidies.

keyActions.action: Signed $18B property tax relief package — SB 2 and SB 3 (2023)
keyActions.notes: Allocated $18B in budget surplus toward lowering school district property tax rates, increasing homestead exemptions, and increasing Franchise Tax exemptions for small businesses. Signed as 'largest property tax cut in Texas history' at the time.

keyActions.action: Signed $10B+ property tax relief package — 2025
keyActions.notes: Raised homestead exemption to $140K ($200K for seniors/disabled). Increased business personal property exemption from $2,500 to $125,000. Permanently reduced business franchise tax by 25% (HB 32).

keyActions.action: Signed strongest bail reform in Texas history — SB 9, SB 40, HB 75 (2025)
keyActions.notes: Restricts cashless bail for violent/repeat offenders. ACLU says it allows judges to deny bail based on vague standards.

keyActions.action: Released 5-Year Economic Development Strategic Plan; created Texas JETI program
keyActions.direction: poleB lean (private sector-first; targeted tax incentive deals rather than broad public investment)
keyActions.notes: JETI provides property tax cuts to companies moving to Texas in exchange for job creation. Emphasis on semiconductor production, aerospace, workforce development at community colleges. Market-driven with targeted incentives — not government-led industrial policy. Texas Enterprise Fund is deal-closing mechanism, not broad public investment program.

keyActions.action: Announced record $148 billion transportation investment — TxDOT 10-year plan
keyActions.notes: 89% of TxDOT budget dedicated to state highway development and maintenance. Public transit and rail receive approximately 2% combined. Abbott quote focused on 'roadways' and 'congestion relief for Texas drivers.'

keyActions.action: Redirected $210M from HHSC (SNAP/Medicaid administrator) to border security
keyActions.direction: poleB (conditional/limited safety net — deprioritized social spending)
keyActions.notes: Redirected hundreds of millions from health and human services to border operations. This created a SNAP/Medicaid application backlog that drew CMS warning letters. Some families waited 6+ months for food assistance.

keyActions.action: Ended federal pandemic unemployment benefits early
keyActions.notes: Opted out of extended federal unemployment programs, citing labor shortage arguments.

keyActions.action: Requested and received SNAP food restrictions waiver
keyActions.direction: poleB (behavioral conditions on safety net benefits)
keyActions.notes: Starting April 1, 2026, SNAP recipients in Texas cannot purchase candy, artificial sweeteners, or high-sugar drinks. Adds behavioral conditions to benefit eligibility.

keyActions.action: Filed ACA lawsuit
keyActions.description: Was the first state AG to file suit against the ACA when it passed. Called it unconstitutional federal overreach.
keyActions.notes: Consistent with ongoing gubernatorial record.

keyActions.action: Sued Obama EPA multiple times over environmental regulations
keyActions.description: Filed multiple suits against EPA climate and clean air regulations. Part of pattern opposing federal environmental oversight.
keyActions.notes: Consistent with gubernatorial executive order pattern.

keyActions.action: Texas Supreme Court case on Ten Commandments
keyActions.description: Successfully advocated for Texas Capitol's Ten Commandments display in Van Orden v. Perry.
keyActions.notes: Background context only.

positionConflicts.topic: Renewable energy vs. Texas as renewable energy leader
positionConflicts.conflict: Abbott frequently touts Texas as the #1 state for wind and utility-scale solar while simultaneously excluding renewables from economic incentives, blaming green energy for the 2021 ERCOT crisis (disputed by experts), backing $18B in natural gas plant subsidies, and directing PUC to penalize renewable projects. Texas leads the US in wind energy output as a market outcome despite Abbott's policy actively disfavoring renewables.
positionConflicts.resolution: Score on policy record, not market output statistics. His policy actions clearly favor fossil fuels.

positionConflicts.topic: Anti-ESG fossil fuel law struck down (February 2026)
positionConflicts.conflict: Abbott signed SB 13 mandating state pension fund divestment from firms 'boycotting' fossil fuels, but a federal judge struck down the law as unconstitutional on First Amendment grounds in February 2026. Abbott has not publicly addressed the ruling.

positionConflicts.topic: Labor endorsements: split between Teamsters and AFL-CIO
positionConflicts.conflict: Abbott received endorsements from Teamsters Joint Council 58 and 80 and several trade unions (plumbers, longshoremen, pipefitters) while the Texas AFL-CIO endorsed his Democratic opponent and called Abbott a failure for workers. Texas remains one of the worst states for labor rights under Abbott: right-to-work enforced, local paid sick leave ordinances preempted, no minimum wage increases.
positionConflicts.resolution: Teamster endorsements likely driven by pipeline/port infrastructure spending, not general labor policy. Score on legislative record and AFL-CIO opposition.

positionConflicts.topic: Housing supply zoning reform vs. general anti-government-mandate posture
positionConflicts.conflict: Abbott signed aggressive pro-density zoning bills in 2025 that override local zoning ordinances — an unusual position for a governor who otherwise champions local government control and opposes government mandates. This is a pragmatic exception apparently driven by housing cost politics.
positionConflicts.resolution: Score the actual policy effect: the bills genuinely loosen zoning. Flag as market-oriented deregulation (supply-side), not government-directed affordability.

positionConflicts.conflict: Abbott describes himself as pro-life and has signed sweeping anti-abortion legislation, but has presided over 55+ executions as governor, granting clemency in only one death penalty case (Thomas Whitaker, 2018) in 11 years despite multiple high-profile cases where credible innocence concerns were raised (Rodney Reed, Melissa Lucio, Robert Roberson).

evidenceSummary.notes: Greg Abbott has an 11-year gubernatorial record plus 13 years as AG — one of the most documented executive records available for any state official. Evidence for all 16 axes is available from primary Tier 1 sources (signed legislation, executive orders, official press releases). No significant evidence gaps. His positions are unusually explicit and consistent — very little ambiguity across any axis. Key 2026 campaign priorities: property tax reform (centerpiece — abolish school property taxes), border security continuation, and defense of school choice. Strongest policy evidence: firearms, school choice, healthcare non-expansion, climate inaction, anti-police-reform. Notable nuance: housing supply zoning reform in 2025 is genuinely supply-liberalizing and is an exception to his otherwise maximum-conservatism posture across most axes.
